title: The Ibadis
hook: the school of Oman and parts of North Africa, which rejects the Kharijite label

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Zaydis of Yemen, and your line: the zaydis. Did the word Shia sound any different to you once you knew it holds more than one house? Day one thousand two hundred four.

A nickname nobody asked for. It sticks in school, or at work, or in the family. It comes from an old story, or from somebody else's mistake, and the person wearing it wants to say: that's not me. Now stretch that across a whole community and a long history. There's a school of Islam, rooted in Oman and in pockets of North Africa, that has been handed a label in other people's books. And its scholars have spent a long time answering, patiently: that's not us. Today, the Ibadis, and the name they refuse.
screen: `A NICKNAME NOBODY ASKED FOR.` → `A WHOLE SCHOOL, ONE LABEL.` → `THAT'S NOT US.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Tradition says the school is named for Abd Allah ibn Ibad, an early figure in Basra, and Ibadis also honor a scholar of that city, Jabir ibn Zayd, as a teacher at their root. So, the Ibadis. Next, the label. In the early civil wars, a group broke away from Ali's camp. Others called them the Khawarij, those who went out. Some of them declared other Muslims unbelievers and treated their blood as lawful. Some writers outside the school filed the Ibadis under that same heading. Ibadi scholars answer that the extremists who killed other Muslims were wrong, and that their own teachers broke from them over exactly that. To an Ibadi, other Muslims stay inside the faith, people to live beside, pray near and trade with. Then, a verse they can point to. The Qur'an says, in Pickthall's words, "neither defame one another, nor insult one another by nicknames." A label used to push someone out of the community is the kind of thing that line warns against. Last, the place. In Oman the Ibadi school has deep roots, with its own scholars, mosques and law. It's also found in parts of North Africa, in desert valleys and on islands, and in communities along the East African coast. Its jurists write their own books of fiqh, with their own methods, and they can tell you exactly where they differ from their neighbors and where they agree. A school with its own name, asking to be called by it.
screen: `NAMED FOR ABD ALLAH IBN IBAD.` · `THE LABEL: THOSE WHO WENT OUT.` · `NOT BY NICKNAMES.` · `OMAN AND NORTH AFRICA.`

segments.voice: The practice: learn one thing about Oman. Here is one, from today: in Oman, the Ibadi school has its own scholars, its own mosques and its own books of law. Say the pair once, slowly: Ibadi, Oman. Let it settle as a name, not a label. Then think of one person you've known only by a label. A coworker, a neighbor, a group in the news. Say their real name, or the name they'd choose, quietly to yourself. If you pray, you can remember them in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
The Ibadis. The school of Oman and parts of North Africa, which counts other Muslims inside the faith and rejects the Kharijite label. Today's word.

Your line: the ibadis of oman. This week took us through other houses: the Ja'fari school, the marja', the seminaries, the turbah, the three times, the Zaydis, the Ibadis. Today, call one person by the name they choose. Day one thousand two hundred four.

howItsDone: Ibadi Muslims, centered in Oman with communities in North Africa and East Africa, follow their own school of law and theology; they reject being called Kharijites and hold that other Muslims remain within the faith.

notes: Editor: 'in book after book' softened; the practice no longer repeats yesterday's map exercise or claims Omani ships reached Zanzibar, and now names one thing from the teach about Oman.
Naming for Abd Allah ibn Ibad and Jabir ibn Zayd as a root teacher, both in Basra: given as 'tradition says'; confirm.
Khawarij glossed 'those who went out' (root kh-r-j): confirm.

Ibadi rejection of the Kharijite label and distance from the Azariqa over killing other Muslims: confirm framing; the script avoids saying Ibadi origins have no link to the early secession, which is debated.
Ibadi view of other Muslims (within the faith, ahl al-qibla): confirm wording.
Communities in North Africa (Mzab in Algeria, Jerba in Tunisia, Jabal Nafusa in Libya) and East Africa (Zanzibar) described generally: confirm.
Omani ships sailing to Zanzibar in the practice: historical, general; confirm acceptable.
